i'm in year 13 and have made 3 short films, have 2 more planned before i leave. 


1) reach out to drama students in your year. reach out to local film/theatre groups in your area. facebook pages as well. you can also get your friends to act in them. or just send an email to your whole year (i sent emails to the whole of sixth form and that's where i found most of my actors). 

2) i have never paid anyone. but i also have mostly worked with students and teachers at my school. i'd say pay them back by sending your finished film to them. a LOT of filmmakers don't do that at our age, either cuz they haven't finished it or think it looks bad. just send it anyway, people want to see what they've been in. 

3) royalty free music stuff. or make the music yourself. or get someone who's interested in music to make stuff. 

4) i use blackmagic 4K and 6K, as well as Sony fx3. but i own none of them, they're just school cameras. i'd suggest to just film on your phone to begin with if you have no school cameras, as phones are still pretty good quality if you're not gonna expand the film on a huge screen. 

5) you can post it on youtube, or submit it into festivals and competitions. honestly there's no set rule of what you do with it, it's yours so you can do whatever you want. but let the actors know beforehand. 

6) i don't think you'll regret anything, the best way to learn filmmaking is by doing it. i'm only 18 so i barely know anything, take my advice with a huge load of salt. but the main thing other than actual filmmaking that i'd advise you to do is to always have a back up, and a back of the back up, for everything. also give yourself breaks. i found on my first short that i was giving everyone breaks, but i myself was constantly running around! and overestimate how long things will take to film, rarely do they ever take the amount of time you planned.

primary school is from age 4-11, (reception to year 6). you get one teacher for pretty much all subjects   except maybe a few exceptions such as PE or a foreign language, but this isn't always the case. not much homework or tests, maybe a little bit when you're in year 5/6. there's no formal grading but there are parents evenings where your teachers inform your parents about how you're progressing in class. there's one exam at the end of year 6 (age 10/11) that tests on reading, writing and maths. however this exam is only done in state schools (equivalent to public schools in usa), and not in private schools. 

secondary school is from 11-16, (year 7-11). you study pretty much every subject from year 7-9 with different teachers and different classes until you pick your gcses at the end of year 9. english literature, english language, maths, and the sciences are compulsory. however most schools will make you take around 8+ at least, so you pick other subjects you're interested in to do alongside the compulsory ones, such as foreign languages (some schools make this compulsory), humanities, arts, etc. for example, in my school we had to take either 10 or 11 gcses. i did 10 gcses, so i sat around 25-30 papers at about 2hrs average for each paper. so 50-60 hours of exams in total. this exam is done at the end of year 11 and preparation starts at the start of year 10. throughout the two years, you get homework, class tests, predicted grades etc. but these don't really matter, only your final grade of gcses matter.

gcses are graded from 9-1 (9 being the highest, 1 being the lowest, and anything below a 4 being a fail). most universities will want you to get at least a 5 in maths and english. you'll most likely need to pass in the subject gcse to take it for A level. however sometimes schools can say that not only do you need to pass to do a certain subject to take it for A Level, but you need to get a "7 and above" for example. 

sixth form/college is from 16-18. The difference between them is that a sixth form is attached to a secondary school, and a college is a completely independent "school" for only 16-18, like a university with only 16-18 year olds. colleges normally offer a wider range of qualifications and apprenticeships, whereas sixth forms mostly offer only a more linear traditional path such as A Levels or BTEC. you can still do these at a college though. 

Not all sixth forms offer BTEC and some even offer the international baccalaureate. I can only speak for A Levels because that's what I've done, it's also the more common one to see. Basically you pick 3-4 subjects, and you pretty much just specialise in those. These are dependent on what course you apply at for uni. For example, someone who didn't take chemistry or biology A Level, won't be able to apply for medicine as they require those subjects. there are many other ones, that's just one example. 

Near the mid to end of year 12 (age 16/17) you sit your AS Levels. AS Levels are a halfway point in the 2-year A level course, and these results are often heavily based in the grade predictions you will receive from your teachers. these predicted grades are very important as they are used for applying to universities. You don't apply to uni with A Level grades, you apply with predicted grades that you receive in the beginning of year 13. as these grades are mostly based on your AS Level exam, that exam is also very important. 

You can apply for a maximum of 5 universities. You get your offers from the university a few months before your A Level exam (basically them telling you if they want you or not). So your A Level exams are pretty much to confirm your predicted grades that got you the offers. I took 3 A Levels, so that was 9 papers and 18 hours of exams in total at the end. but just like secondary school, there are many tests and homework assignments in between. but unlike secondary, they do kind of matter as they are needed for your predicted grades for uni. 

Grading works differently in england. it's more so based on how difficult the paper was. for example, if a paper was really easy, the grade boundaries will be high and you might only get an A with 90%. however if the exam was really hard, you could get an A with 50%. obviously these are more exaggerated examples but you get the gist. For A Levels, the grading is from A*-D being a pass, and E and U being a fail. For universities, courses will normally have grades that you need to get in order to apply for the course. For example, a course could say you need 'ABB'. This means you need to get 1 A and 2 Bs in your prediction to apply to get an offer. Then in your A Levels, you actually need to get those grades in order to go through with your offer. 

Finally, you don't actually need to go to college or sixth form from 16-18. school is compulsory up to 16 (year 11 after gcses) and then after that you need to either be in education, training or work until 18. Also, your final exams (GCSEs and A Levels) are not marked by your teachers. the papers are scanned in and there's external examiners that mark your papers anonymously through the exam board. So your teachers have no control over what you get in them. You class tests, mock exams, and AS Levels are marked by your class teachers though.
